title: Christian Parker: "We're Still Enrolled in the Program" | Press Conference
text: Uh Joe Hoy, Dallas Morning News. Um you said earlier that this was going to be like a master's degree for these guys with, you know, joint practices done and two more preseason games left. Where are they in that master's degree path right now? >> Uh we're still enrolled in the program. You know, we're making progress for sure. Um a lot of um tests have been passed, but it's you know, some more more work to go. >> I know with regard to Caleb DS, you said earlier that he's been as advertised, but has there been anything about him so far that surprised you? Anything about his game or the way he's worked that surprised you at all? Uh, no. I mean, I Well, I mean, maybe his just his competitiveness, you know, he has a he has a streak on the field. You know, obviously you don't know that until you're in those competitive environments with somebody. Um, but he definitely has a fire to him and an edge deal Cowboys just picking back on Caleb DS. Uh, certainly he's gone against CD in Georgia practice and Chris Lave yesterday. Just talk about what you see. That's what you're talking about, the competitive not backing down to those situations. What can he learn with those matchups? >> Yeah, I mean, you learn from every matchup regardless of who you're going against. I think that, you know, it's been a lot that he's been real tight in coverage. Some plays he's made, some plays he hasn't. I think even the good plays, there's something you can fix and correct off of those, whether it's footwork, hand placement, eyes, the situation that you're in and what to expect with the stem and the release and all those things. So, every rep is a learning experience for all the guys, especially young players. >> Can you talk about your relationship with uh Von going back to Denver and how what do you envision for him in this defense? Yeah, I mean Von was um you know he was kind of an honorary member of NoFly Zone that that predated me. So he was always around the DBs and everything. Um you know ultimate professional um phenomenal teammate and obviously he can still you know get after the quarterback and play at a high level on as an all down player. So we're not really putting a cap on you know what what could be this year. Uh we're going to let that kind of handle itself but um we definitely feel good about that edge room and feel good about the addition. Christian to ESPN on game day. What's your demeanor? Are you any different on a game than practice? It looked like, you know, when when the defense came over, you kind of wanted to be on your tablet and see things and then communicate that way. Can you just kind of walk us through how you want to approach how you were on game day? >> Yeah, I mean, I'm I'm pretty I'm pretty calm most times regardless. I think I have a little more uh fire on the practice field. But I think that's the environment to have that. Um on game day, it's about the players. So I try to stay as calm as possible. Um and and communicate clearly and directly, you know, with the assistants and then with the players as well. Um have to be, you know, more analytical and and go through the process and and kind of separate myself a little bit, if you will. Um, so I try to, you know, be the one that's kind of staying even killed and the emotions of the game are going to be so rampant and, um, you know, somebody has to kind of be level-headed, you know, so, you know, the talk and stuff that kind of happens on the practice field when you're kind of in close quarters with the opponent and everything else. Um, that kind of, you know, uh, deletes itself on on game day. Um, just try to stay level-headed and calm as possible. >> Was that the same when you were a position coach? Were you that way, too, or were you more fired up? >> No, I was the same way as a position coach. But I think on game day it's about the players and you know they're the ones that are out there. They're the ones that are experiencing all the emotions of the game. Um the crowd, the momentum, uh the personal battles within a play, you know, so you have to be the one that whether it's good or bad, you're kind of bringing things back to neutral, you know, relative to energy and and the message that's given. >> John with the athletic, uh what do you like about being on the sidelines, I guess, versus potentially, you know, being up at the box calling the defense? Uh, I've been on the sideline most years as the, you know, as the, uh, DB coach, so I know I can, I can see what I need to see from down there. I like being in the flow of the game. Um, being able to communicate directly with the coaches, with the players if need be. Um, so I think there's advantages to both for sure, you know, whether you're up or down, but um, I know that's kind of always been my my feel uh, in that matter. >> And then the two joint practices obviously different, but what would you say is the biggest thing that you were able to get out of those two practices? Uh the main thing is you're seeing two different schemes, you know, so you count the now, you know, we we see two schemes in the games, right? Seattle, Arizona. We play the Saints next week, but to be able to see the Rams and their offense, see the Saints and their offense, very different in terms of how they present problems and how to solve them. So whether it's motions, formations, personnel, um just overall philosophy of what they do. I think that's the most important thing you try to get out of those. >> Tommy Arcway.com. You said a couple times that you're ready to call plays and you prepared for it for a while, but finally doing it for the first time on Saturday. What was that like? Did it live up to your expectations? >> Yeah. Yeah, it felt good. I think our operation um from a coaching staff standpoint was very smooth. Information in the box, the communication on the sideline, everything between series, during the series, um it was quiet on the headset, which was a good thing. Um and uh was able to get in a good flow. that first drive they go 80 yards is a long drive they score and then 76 yards the rest of the way. How did you see your guys settle in after that? >> Yeah, I think you know we just had to play cleaner football. You know I think that there's always going to be the emotions the first time being out there again. Um you know so we just had to settle in and just play ball. You know I don't think that the first drive was necessarily uh sloppy other than the penalties. Um and we had you know an eye discipline problem on one play but I think overall the guys were really disciplined. They were connected with each other. Uh they played the style that we want to play. Uh, so we have to continue to build on that. >> Hey Christian, Patrick Bo, Dallas Cowboys.com. Uh, because he wasn't able to participate last offseason because he was recovered from that ACL injury. It's fair to say Simone Rebel is kind of in his rookie off seasonason over these past several months up to this point. Iron sharpens iron that matters. Another one out there with Chris Lobby yesterday. Where do you see him in his process, his development, and what can he be for your defense? >> Yeah, I think he's uh he's developing nicely. The first thing is is uh he runs to coaching. So, he's always looking for ways to improve. It could be a good rep, it could be a bad rep, it could be a rep that he wasn't even in on. Um, he's always looking for ways that, you know, how can he catch up from the mental side of the game. And I've mentioned that before. It's just, you know, consistency. When you have young players, you, you know, they're going to reach a height where you're starting to see, okay, yeah, it's getting better, but then it's a point that that's not good enough. And then you want to see them, you know, break through that glass ceiling because nobody out there is going to have any tape on their helmet that says, I'm a rookie, I'm a first year player. we expect a standard of performance for everybody. He's reached that level. we expect better things from him and he's he's been reaching those expectations and now it's just about the kind of eliminating the the 501st dates if you will you know certain formations and motions and situations and calls and routes and just trying to continue to learn from those to kind of build his uh intellectual bank um from pre- snap and during the play uh mindset so we can continue to perform because he has all the traits you want and he's made great strides in terms of the mental part of the game and having that confidence in himself. Babe Loenberg, Cowboys radio 105.3 the fans. So Christian, I know we're not game plan. You're not game planning in the preseason, but once you get there, are you a plays versus players guy in terms of are you defending the scheme and then looking to take away players or do you go into it looking to take away players and then figuring out how you want to attack the scheme? >> I think it depends on who you're playing. Um, you know, certain offenses, you know, you got to figure out what what world they're living in, right? You know, certain offenses are players over plays. They might try to find 10 different ways to get a guy the ball. Some are going to be very true to their their schematics and what they try to build from a play standpoint, from a run pass, play action pass, screen game, making marrying everything up. Uh so I think you just have to know who you're going against. You know, I think the first thing is handling your business in-house first. So selfcout is very important. What are we doing well? Because it doesn't matter if we know what they're doing if we don't know, you know, what we're doing. So, handling that first and then being able to kind of make the make the team play uh left-handed, whether that's affecting the quarterback, the offensive coordinator, the offensive line, whatever the case might be. >> Dan Greenspan, Associated Press. Uh Don Venezer, who was ejected from practice yesterday, second time in camp that it happened for throwing a punch. How do you get him to walk that line without crossing it? >> Yeah, I think we've had a lot of uh good conversations about that. Um we're on the same page. Donovan knows that, you know, we're a better defense when he's on the field. I think that's where it starts is um the connection with your teammates and being available. Um you know, we're going to play with an edge. That's what we're going to do. Um but we got to find ways to not cross that line and and stay together and stay neutral in that regard. So um good learning experience for him yesterday in terms of just being able to kind of uh maintain his composure and poise. Um but we certainly have been encouraged with him and and his play and his maturity and growth this uh training camp. >> Hey Christian, Jeff Gold with Fox 4. Two questions for you if I could. BT Jordan, his impact on your pass rushers, what has that looked like and how important was his input in the Von Miller side? >> Uh, yeah, I think his impact is uh has been phenomenal. You know, he his uh his contributions inside and outside, you know, on the field and off um with individual players collectively with those guys. I think having the rushes one mentality really speaking to that. Um, and being able to develop rushers individually on where they are and what their fast ball needs to be and what the change up needs to be. Um, I think he's been great. Um, and obviously, you know, there were multiple relationships with Van, you know, outside the building that kind of led to to that happening. Um, but he obviously he he definitely had a factor in that. >> Last week, spoke with Marcus Dixon. Uh, he said that you hardly sleep. That's how dedicated you are to the job. How limited is the amount of sleep. What does that look like? Uh, >> I don't really want to talk about that. Um, yeah, it's not something I'm necessarily proud of, but um, you know, the the job has to get done and you kind of go down a rabbit hole sometimes and you look up at the clock and you know, you miss that time. So, uh, you try to get as much preparation as you can during the week and then, uh, catch up at the end. >> Hey, coach Nicole Hutcherson, Dallas Cowboys.com. Mayor's Le foul, switching positions pretty much having to learn the pass rush aspect of it. Where have you seen him kind of grow in terms of that and where do you feel like he should take the next step? Yeah, I think Maris the first thing is, you know, the difference between he's had some experience being on the edge before. Um, the main thing is the immediate contact. You know, things happen faster there. I think that he's made great strides and just controlling the C area with his hands and his power. Um, and being able to kind of figure out those blocks and everything as they kind of come to play with power. Um, his coverage skills are, you know, that's second nature to him because he's been in those situations. But um him figuring out like the blocking schemes and tackle sets and all those things that are involved with being there um while still being able to be versatile for us, you know, he's made a lot of great strides in that um and we're continuing to develop him and we've been happy with his progress. >> Brad Sham Cowboys radio 1053 the fan. Ready Stewart's an interesting guy. He doesn't seem to be physically suited for any one particular thing, but he does a bunch of things kind of well. What did you think of him when you came in and what have you seen in his growth? >> Yeah, the the main thing with Ready is you see the play style and the urgency he plays with. You know, it's really important to him. He's willing to be physical. He's a first responder in a lot of situations in the run game and the pass game as a as a zone aware player. Um we were able to kind of spotlight, you know, moonlight him a little bit at safety as well, which kind of went into the nickel job category with a lot of those things being similar. Um and he's done a a really good job for us in training camp. you know, I think that uh he's always willing. Um you know, he's he's smart and uh he really knows how to communicate and connect with his teammates. Um it was good to see him make a play on the ball yesterday as well and and get that sack on uh on the last game, but you know, he's continuing to develop and we're happy with him, too. >> Is there anything he does better than you thought before you got your hands on him that he'd be able to do? >> Yeah, I didn't know. You know, you never know um a player's processing ability. I think that's something that you can see sometimes on film, but you don't really know because you don't know what they're being told, what they're being coached, the details of the scheme all the time. I think he's a fast processor. Um, you can make sideline adjustments with him. They make sense for him to kind of uh carry to the field. Um, and he has a high care factor. >> When you first got into coaching, did you write down goals at all and say, "I want to do this at this age," or anything like that? >> Uh, yeah, I did. Um, and then I quickly realized that th those those things don't matter, you know, to be honest with you. So early on when I started off like, yeah, you want to, you know, I was 21 my first year coaching, right? So it was like, you know, I want to be this by 25, this by 30. Uh, you know, I didn't think I was maybe going to get into the league until I was like, you know, 35 years old cuz, you know, only 32 teams. It's hard to get the internships and get around and how you going to make those connections. And then you start getting going and you realize that those timelines don't matter. um you know, it's it's it's bigger than that and it's just about putting the work in and um trusting God and and obviously taking advantage of opportunities when they're presented to you. So, I kind of got off that train pretty quick. >> And then when you interview the jobs, either position coaches or defense boarding the last couple years? Um did was age ever mentioned to you and brought up at all from the people talking to you? Yeah, I think it it comes up in the in the realm of like, you know, how do you deal with players older than you, you know, and and kind of how do those things go? Um, again, you know, I don't know anything else cuz I've always been young, so it's not like I have, uh, you know, maybe I'll be able to answer that, you know, in 20 years or so. But, um, yeah, sometimes it comes up and I think that, you know, at the end of the day, players want you to um, be able to help them get better and they want to know that you care about their development and you care about winning. And I think that no matter what your age is, that's all that matters. You know, if they know that you can connect with them, if you can help them improve their game, um, and we can help each other win games together, then that's all that matters. >> You mentioned rushing as one, uh, from pass rush standpoint. What goes into that and how much is it curating a specific combination of guys that you want to see with different skill sets? >> Yeah, I think the combination of players starts in practice. Um it starts with, you know, whether we're, you know, you're rushing straight, those guys are naturally feeling each other in terms of the the paths that you're taking. Um whether it's, you know, orchestrated games that we call or patterns in the pressure. Um but guys just not being selfish, you know, and and having that mentality that, you know, if you're supposed to be here, then you got to be there because that's setting this up. if I'm supposed to be picking this or you know whatever the call is and whatever that might be. Just having that uh mentality where what we're rushing with vision um and we're able to um not be selfish in that mentality where we're giving up you know free B gap escapes or giving up the edge quickly. Um but guys understand what their role is in the rush and at some point they're going to have that one-on-one, you know, that we desire. Um but as long as everybody has that same mentality of everybody eating together, uh then we'll have success. >> Thank you.

title: Klayton Adams: "Competition Is the Main Function of Our Program" | Press Conference
text: Joe Hoyt, Dallas Morning News. You've had more play calling stuff than you called against the Rams and obviously Shai has been sprinkling in some things. How's that been going for you and how have you kind of evolved and learned from that process? So >> Yeah, I've I've really enjoyed doing it. Definitely learned a bunch kind of about myself cuz there's times sometimes when you're looking at the call sheet and you don't really love something and then something pops in your head, you know, and and it kind of gives you like, all right, here's the go-to things with a certain down and distance that you're very comfortable with. Um Yeah, no, I felt like it's it's it's been a great education for me. >> You guys have a starter for Saturday yet and if not, just how did Joe Milton respond to being the second guy last week and what did you think of his play? >> Uh I mean, we we've had discussions about it. We haven't made any definite decision about this weekend, but I'd say just based on the way that he played, he definitely responded the right way. Um I think Shady said it after the game, but he looked under control and and to be honest that's what we've seen most of camp. And just like any player, there's going to be a couple of up down up moments and down moments and what we've seen mostly from Joe has been has been growth and consistency. >> Barry Horn, The Dallas Cowboys. You talked about Tyler Guyton camp and his development. What have you seen from him after getting challenged early on about his position? >> Uh I would say, you know, I it's always kind of one of those things where in the back of my mind I'm like, I'm just not going to say anything. I'm just going to kind of let the days go by and and see where we're at at the end. I think we've seen much more consistency from him. I don't know what training camp was like his rookie season, but my understanding was that he was kind of in and out of the lineup and that was the same thing as last year and so knock on wood, but I'm happy to be to to the point that we're at in training camp and him being able to put practices back-to-back and they all haven't been perfect, but they haven't been for any of our guys and so, you know, just just trying to find consistency and confidence in his play has been kind of a special journey watching him because I'm proud of the work that he's put in and the mental toughness that he's developed and some of the maturity the maturation process that he's gone through all the way through the off season. >> Putting him in competition was that a motivating factor for him, you think? >> I'm sure it probably was. You know, just in regards to to putting him in competition. I mean, like to me that's it's the main function of our program here. You know, Shady says it all the time, but to me that's just life, you know, and and anything that we do when you have great competition like watching our offense and our defense go against each other. It just makes everybody better. And so, one of the things that we've said in the offensive room is just being outward focused with some of those things of yeah, you're competing against each other, but when you can truly be happy for another guy's growth and and use that as motivation for your own growth, that's when that's when we can be operating at a really high level to me higher than other teams. >> I'm Todd Archer for ESPN. Does anything Malik Davis do surprise you? >> No. Uh simply put, no. He Malik is awesome and he's got great run instincts. He never pouts about reps. He just goes in when it's his turn and does it good. >> And then I I was watching the Mike that thing and I think I might have heard it twice, maybe not. What's the hot dog fridge? >> Well, it's something that I'm working on here, you know, kind of in the back of my mind is is, you know, how can you really have a break room or a snack room if you don't have a hot dog fridge, you know, and and you and if you're going to have a hot dog fridge, you've got to have high quality hot dogs in it. And if you're going to have high quality hot dogs in it, we've got to have brioche buns and maybe some pretzel buns. So, these are all things that we're working on. Maybe an industrial-size 7-Eleven hot dog roller. I don't know. I don't know, but um these are just things I roll around in the back of my mind. >> I like a sponsorship deal with you. >> [laughter] >> What do you put on your hot dog? >> Uh you know, I I am I'm a huge fan of just mayonnaise, mustard, and pickles. And then one of the things I learned from going to Disneyland with my kids cuz I I was trying to steam the bun. I was trying to toast the bun. And the guy at Disneyland goes, "No, man. Put it in the bun and wrap it in foil and let the hot dog steam the bun." It's been revolutionary. I'm not a mayonnaise guy. Yeah. No, no mayonnaise for me. I'm from America. >> Speaking of the mic stuff, what's the best thing that didn't make the cut? >> Oh gosh. Yeah, there's a lot probably stuff that would have just been bleeps running for 25 or 30 seconds at a time. Um I don't generally run real real hot, but uh there are I do sometimes say some things that you wouldn't be able to put on social media. So, uh definitely can't repeat them here. Um but yeah, probably that type of thing. >> And then with George Pickens, you know, I mean we see the big plays out there. We We saw him obviously last season, too. But from your perspective, what do you What do you think is the next step for George Pickens? >> Um you know, I I think uh whether whether we would want to move him around a bunch in games or not, to me that's kind of a week-to-week thing. But I think just the process of of putting him in other spots and letting him run some different routes because I think that creates more of like a uh a 360 understanding of our offense. And that's to me where we need to head with him is, "Oh, you know what? We are running a deep cross over here. That's why I'm running an M or on the boundary." I I just think creating a deeper understanding of everything that we're doing and and even in the run game, too. You know, you you get into the slot and you've got some different rules. And those are the things I think would be good for him that we're trying to kind of slowly introduce him to. >> Hey Clayton, so I'm going to lead with the dad joke here. One guy that's not hot dogging it on the field, KaVontae Brown. So, are you guys have you guys seen enough from KaVontae Brown throughout camp and of course, you know, as he translates it onto the field with those two touchdowns against the AFC hopefuls, is he now in the conversation of potentially being bubble wrapped and and if not, is he going to be on a limited rep count? How do you guys negotiate that with the you know, young man who's still trying to prove himself, but you guys also have seen a lot from him up to this point. >> Yeah, I I those are all kind of discussions for for the personnel type meeting, but my my thought process with with young guys that are battling to make the team is that we have to give them opportunities to show consistency and show that you can do it on a week in week out basis. So, that I I don't feel any different with Cam than I do with any of the other guys cuz, you know, this week it might be somebody else that shows up and makes a couple of plays and you know, to this is a pretty competitive roster and and specifically a pretty competitive receiver room and you know, there there's a you're going to have to be able to do it every week to make this team and so, that's what we're going to need to see from all of them. >> And really quickly, what does it say about Cam's skillset and his his mental fortitude to be able to produce regardless of who the quarterback is? >> I I think that the the quarterback room in general likes to to know body language, receivers that can kind of communicate with their back turned. And those are things I think they're very comfortable with Cam on is this there's a certain level of consistency to his route running, there's a certain level consistency to his releases when he gets pressed. There's certain things that he does with his body at the top of the route that that you can anticipate where he's going to be and when he's going to be there. And Cam's done a nice job of those things. >> Tommy R. Stouts Cowboys.com. Going back to Arizona Saturday, is there any sentimental value in you for you with that? >> No, not really. No. Yeah, I mean they get a nice grass field on the indoor. I we had nice times doing training camp out there. I do think about that some and I still have obviously um my wife and my family and I have good friends in the valley there. Um but yeah, no, not at this point with Jonathan Gannon gone and >> All right, then. How would you evaluate Terence Steele's training camp this year? >> Uh I would say it's been up and down. Um you know, he and I had a good conversation about that this morning of how we continue to try to find consistency and um he's a guy that's going into year seven and he's never going to ask for a day off and he's never going to ask for a break. And so, we're just searching for ways to help him and uh help him play at his best and and most consistent. >> Rihanna Aldridge, CBS News Texas. Coach, uh Rondale Moore recently talked about remembering this time last year just trying to stay relevant in where you're talking about wide receiver five spot and talked about how thankful he is to be where he is now. And he said he got there cuz he feels like he's done stuff the right way. From a coach's standpoint, how have you seen him doing it the right way? >> Yeah, I I said this about uh Flo, I think a few weeks ago, but it's uh Flo kind of got to the point maybe week three or four last year where he became like a a sentient player where you explain the details to him, you kind of give him the black and white. You want to make things as black and white as you can for the players so they can kind of have an idea and understanding. But when guys hit that hit that certain level of understanding where they're like, I know exactly why this is this route is complementing this route. I know exactly where it is in the read and I know when there's gray area what I can and I can't do. Um when when he hit that level, his confidence, bang, you know, it grew. And I think it was probably the Jets game where where he started coming out and really getting the opportunities and making the plays. But you know, that's where we're trying to kind of push a lot of these guys. I always talk about that that fourth install. Um I think you got to get past that before you can can reach that level as a player, but it's definitely been fun to watch with him because it's just continued and grown um both from his development in the meeting room with with Junior Adams and Bravo. Those guys do a great job with him, but it it's fun to watch players grow on their own when they hit that level and he's doing that and and I love the guy. He he's a he's a great dude to be around and awesome player. >> Dan Greenspan Associated Press. Going back to Terrance for a second. Brian said yesterday his pad level hasn't been where you guys have wanted it. What what goes into addressing that uh when you have you're you're jumping in and out of pads and and trying to balance different things at this point of the year? >> Well, I think uh you know, in in today's NFL different than probably 10 or 12 years ago, there's there's uh a lot of different uh medical things that guys are doing to try to make sure that their flexibility and their explosiveness and that they're rested properly. I think we've run a great camp in terms of that and putting guys in position to do that and you know, we're trying to create competition and at every level and so some of it is is hard to get guys a few reps off. You know, that's one of the things that we're potentially looking into is is how do we get him in year seven in a mode where he can be at his best all the time? What's the right workload for that? So, those are questions that in my mind I'm trying to answer. >> And the other thing I wanted to ask you was, how do you go about developing swing tackles having guys that you feel comfortable you could put in at either left or right during a game? >> Yeah, uh so that it's a really good question because if you draft a guy in the first round or whatever just hypothetically, you're probably thinking I need to put him at the spot and I need to keep him there and he needs to go in and and be able to play that spot. Uh when you're bringing someone in to potentially swing, you have to play them on both sides a fair amount and so I think that there's several different stages to it. And I think this applies to a lot of different positions, not just the offensive line, but the stagger that goes into the right side and the left side needs to be worked a lot. When you start a guy as a swing player, I like to think of it as at least a week on one side and then at least a week on the other side. For example, Nate Thomas right now is in the mode in camp where he's going to play some on the right. T.J. Bass is a interior swing guy that's played a lot of left guard and center. He's now taking reps on the right. So, developing some of the I don't know if if the science community will kill me if the muscle memory is not a thing, but that's what we used to say when when I was a kid. Um but developing that and you're doing something with your left hand that you're used to doing with your right hand. Those type of things. I think as a player gets uh more experience in his career, for example, I had a guy that was in year 12 in Arizona who was a swing player. I could throw him on both sides in the same series, and that was good to be able to do that for him. I wouldn't want to do that with a young player, even though sometimes that happens. >> Jeff Kolb with Fox Sports. I know you claim that you see how much Dak Prescott takes on his plate with this job. Brian spoke last week about leadership council maybe taking a little bit of that leader burden off of Dak. Do you think that's important and can you see benefits of >> Yeah, 100%. Um you can't survive with just one good leader if you want a uh player-led locker room. And so, you know, what Shady's done such a good job of is, you know, we ask these questions in the off-season. Sometimes we find answers, sometimes we don't, but how do you develop leadership? And to me, it's no different than how do you develop a position coach out of a QC guy or how do you develop a coordinator out of a position coach? You have to give them opportunities to do it, and then you have to give them immediate feedback after they're doing it. And so, when you put a person in a position to lead, you have to allow them to lead, and then you have to be able to give them feedback. And it's just like anything else. I mean, there's coaching that's involved with it. Here's what you did well. Here's what I think that probably you need to rethink going into the next time based on the response that you got. >> Thank you, everyone. >> Thank you, Barry. >> Yep. Thank you.

title: Nick Sorensen: "When You Produce, You Get More Opportunities" | Press Conference
text: Uh, Joe Hoyt, Dallas Morning News. Uh, Shaddy said special teams performance wasn't up to his standard against the Seahawks. Um, how do you get to that standard and and what did you see as the main thing preventing you from getting that standard? >> Yeah, it definitely wasn't up to our standard. You know, we turn the ball over, we don't win the net net punt or the starting position for kickoff. Uh, the cool thing is we get another game. We had a joint practice yesterday. We get another game after that. So, we get to be pointed on this different guys that we want to see and it's exciting because we can be better. And there were certain things that showed up, you know, we practice those, we do it more, and just guys when they get the opportunities, let's go make plays. And if they do, they get another opportunity and after that if you don't, then hey, let's see somebody else and I'm excited to see us get better this week. >> And uh, special teams obviously is a major decider for back into the roster stuff. Jonathan Mingo had a, you know, chase down tackle. How much does that when you were kind of voicing to who you want maybe in the back end, how much does that matter to you? >> That's elite finish. I mean, it's exceptional effort. I think that affects the whole team. It was the first clip that Shaddy showed to the team. Uh, the next time we were all together after that game doing the recap. I mean, that type of effort, that's what you want everywhere in football and anywhere in life. I mean, it was just really cool to see that from Mingo, just the effort that he gave cuz he won early. He did a really good job versus the vice getting out of bounds. He almost stacked him and made that play, but to see him, you know, get pushed past when the returner stepped up and be able to catch him, that was awesome. It was cool. >> Yeah, I'm Michelle with The Athletic. Uh, you mentioned the joint practices. What what do you get out of those? Uh, you know, both of them. I know they're both kind of different, both of them. What were you able to get out of those >> I I love the joint practices. I think everybody does because now you get to compete against somebody else. You start to get to know each other. It's like anything, you need to change it up a little bit. You don't know exactly what they're going to do, you know, um, you've got different players. You start to get to know the guys that you go against without realizing it, you know, as a player. So, for us it's that and then just the added intensity of it's our team against their team. You know what I mean? And for us, what we focus on is punt. And so what we do is we do the punt rushes. You know, we go with ones, twos, and threes against the Rams against with the New Orleans. We just did the ones and twos, but you get the gunner work versus the vice. And then we both get to do both sides of it. So, it's really good work for both of us and you know, communicating beforehand with the coordinator helps a lot. So, we're all on the exact same page. We're really efficient with it. We've got clear boundaries of you know, Halo protecting the punter so you're not going to have any injuries with positions that you don't We don't We don't want anyone hurt, but we don't We want to get our work without getting guys hurt. So, it was really good. >> And then Caleb Downs, the punt returner, what do you think of him? >> He's been great. He's been great. We're obviously We're not using him in the game, but he's tracked the ball well. He gets catches every day when it's a punt period. He He does get reps also as a PP so I make sure that he gets down there and gets a live rep um early before he's up. Um he's been great. He's been catching them off post-practice, too. >> Hey Nick, Patrick Walker, Dallas Cowboys.com. So, obviously as a group, you want special teams to improve, but when you talk about certain guys like Jonathan Mingo, Marquise Bell had some effort plays as well. What are some of those guys that you've seen uh stand out that you're going to try to lean more on as you guys try to figure out who your aces are on special teams? >> I think it's it's There's a lot of guys, really. I mean, you named Mingo. He's been doing good. I Speed's been doing really good lately, too. Not just in the game, but also in the both joint practices. So, we just see these guys compete, you know? And then there's There's a lot of guys that are going for it. We just want as a unit us to be tied together. I I I don't question the effort. That's awesome. So, now we just clean up some technique stuff and how we need to play blocks, how we need to block better, and I think it'll come together. I'm just excited to get this next game. >> Jeff Kolb with Fox 4, Nick. Obviously, K'Von Thibodeaux has been a multi-time Pro Bowler and one of the better returners in the league. Can you talk about his progress and what is the competition behind him look like with the other returners? >> Yeah, we got a bunch of guys that that can catch. Like I said, you know, Mingo's been catching punts and we got Caleb Downs. We've also got a number of guys that get work at kick returner, too, but Turpin's a stud, like you said, he's a Pro Bowler. Expect a big year out of him. >> I'm Nick Eatman, Archer of the ESPN. A little a little different, but I think I saw Lenoir working as a holder a little bit earlier a couple weeks ago, maybe. How would How do you look for your backup holder, and is that job harder than people know? >> Yes. You look for guys that you think are can catch and put it down. I think you can learn it. I only know that cuz I had to do it like as a backup. You just need to have We would call it pair and a spare. So, if you get two injuries, really any position you're you can be in a tough position, but we always like to have a couple guys that snap. So, you just you start in the meeting, has anyone ever held, have you ever kicked, have you ever punted? So, most of the guys all think they can punt. Like, Jake Ferguson is punting after practice, and you know, you you don't do it often, but you need to have a few guys that can actually snap, get you out of a game, short and long. So, we we try and use a lot of guys, but as snappers, usually if you can catch the ball well, you think a guy's athletic in hands, usually it's those skill guys, whether it's offense or defense, and and so, we're training Flo. He's one guy that we're train We've got a few guys that we train every year, just cuz you got to have it just in case. >> Jake said he has the Wisconsin record for longest punt or something like that. >> Yeah, that was a It was like 60-mph winds. And it was Yeah. But he he's got a strong leg. He can kick it pretty good. And and Hunter's really good at a lot of that stuff, too. He'd never snapped it before or held, and he's pretty good at them. We got a number of guys that You just got to do it every other day post practice, four or five, get our specialists working with them, give them some tips that they see, and you know, you just always got to be prepared. >> Does he like the ball tilted or either way, anything like that? >> Yeah, it's pretty standard. He he he lets them know. That's the first thing we do. We have those guys show them exactly how they do it. Brandon's watching the whole time. I talk to the which guys you think are the best, and we kind of go pecking order, and those guys are on the depth chart. They'll be up there and just so they know that they got to get their post practice work just like the returners. >> Brad Sham with the Cowboys radio 105.3 fan. What's your When a guy in a preseason game like Cale did last week gets a couple of penalties early do you have a do you have an inclination to sit him down for a while or do you feel under those circumstances you need to throw him back out there and keep him >> For me it's different. Cuz we only had 19 special teams plays. There were only 13 big four plays. So it was really really light in the numbers. Usually usually in the high 20s and hopefully you're hitting low 20s around 20 low 20s. So we go into the game with a plan. Maybe these three guys are one and done. Maybe these guys I want to Carlos I want to get two reps with him. So we talk about every guy every row. It's it's a lot more work for us with that than saying oh that was bad. No no we usually go in with a plan that has to be adjusted completely based on are they playing a ton on offense or defense too. So I don't let the effects of the game of what they did. That plan is usually happened. The only thing that might be if we get a lot of punts earlier we haven't gotten a lot. The guy hasn't been in it for a while then we okay we want to see this guy. It's more of that than the actual result of the play. Mhm. >> Anything else? >> Malik Davis guy that came in last year halfway through training camp. Obviously seems like you guys trust and respect him a lot. How much do you trust respect him and appreciate him? >> A lot. And remember the preseason game last year he blew somebody up you know on running down as the PP. And all he does is fix things like he's very coachable. He's very trustworthy. He goes 100 miles an hour every day. Um he just he he's self-made. You know he's a guy that you like working with but he also makes plays. He's productive. That's the main thing he produces and that's that's how you stay in the league is produce right? Make plays and then you'll keep playing or you'll get more opportunities and then you'll play longer. So, when you produce you get more opportunities and then when you get those opportunities do it again, shoot, you're on the team and you're doing it in games. And he's been doing that. >> All right. Thank you, guys. >> Yeah. Thanks, guys.

title: Dave Fipp Media Availability | 2026 Training Camp Day 15
text: Oh, man. I can't believe I'm here. I'll just say that. Just been coaching in this league, there's nothing like it. I feel like a kid in a candy store. I was thinking about that before I came down here. When I was a kid, my brothers and I we'd ride our bike down the street a couple miles away. We'd be a little candy. We'd you know, you'd share. Hey, can I get one of yours? You'll give me one of mine. Uh it was incredible, but it's the same thing today. I feel very, very fortunate lucky working for a head coach that I'm working for, being part of this organization, working with these players out on the practice field. There's really nothing like it for me. So, I'm thankful to be here and whatever questions you guys got, I'll do my best. >> What was your candy of choice? >> Uh it was Coke bottles, the little Coke gummies, Coke bottle gummies. Those things are pretty strong. The red jelly beans, those ones too. That was it. Yeah. >> You'll have a lot to say, I guess, it comes out of special teams, the guys on the back end of the roster of how much they're contributing on special teams. Uh do you feel kind of like a linchpin in that way of in the decision-making process of you know, if it works, what do you think of this guy, that guy? >> Yeah, I think I tell the players. I mean, in the old days I felt like yeah, there was a handful of guys that they just made the roster on special teams and I feel like time over the last handful of years has changed a little bit. We've had more injuries collectively probably as a league. You're playing more players throughout the course of a year. I tell the players now like you're going to make the the team probably in two phases. You're going to have to play on offense and special teams or defense and special teams and I know this, the more that you can do, the better in modern football. If all you can do is play on special teams, you're going to have to be really, really special to make it just on that. Now, you have to have some function. Now, if you're very, very good on special teams and you can help a little bit on defense, you know, you got a chance or you're really, really good on defense and don't do much on special teams, you still got a chance there, but I think for the most part we're looking for guys who can help in all areas. Um and uh we end up playing a lot of players throughout the course of a year. Uh when they ask my opinion on guys, I'm going to give them my opinion and tell them to the best of my knowledge what I think on how a guy will play for us. >> Has there been a guy or two who stood out, who's taken that message [clears throat] to heart? Maybe a younger guy who's understood how much how valuable special teams is to getting them on the >> Yeah, I I think uh you know, the one thing we got uh you know, we we are replacing some good players and there's also a lot of good competition out there. I would definitely say that. And there's a lot of players that a lot of positions like linebacker, there's four guys probably. You got Eric Conner, you got Botsy, you got Reeder, and you got Agbongbemi uh these four players that can all play. Uh you got Hunter's a young guy, the other guys have all played in the league. Um and uh it's very very competitive. So, you're looking for who's going to play the most or be the most dependable player, who can help the most on defense and special teams, probably the combination of the two. Um so, that's a competitive spot. I think the wide receiver spot's very very competitive. You got Martin, you got Black, you got uh Lucky Jackson who's made some plays. Um and these are all down the line guys. And then obviously those guys above them, you have the returner position with Kennedy and Dorch, really a punt returner and Lovett fitting into that a little bit. But really probably Kennedy and Dorch right now in my opinion. Um so, there's a number of positions. The safety position, you know, is really up in the air right there, who's going to play there. Obviously with the injuries to the safety position, who's coming back and So, yeah, there's a lot to process, but >> Wanted to follow up on Hunter. We see you match him up a lot with Nowaski in in practice and that seems like a pretty good challenge with a guy that's proven at this level and all signs like the rookie's holding his own. I'm just curious how much he's he's caught your eye, how I may more advanced he might be than you anticipated coming from Morgan State. >> Yeah, I I would say he's definitely caught our eye. He's caught everybody's eye, I know that. You know, the challenge for young guys is and we we match guys up with a lot of different players. We do that. We do veteran on veteran, veteran on rookie, you know, smaller guy on bigger guy, bigger guy on smaller guy. You're trying to gain a lot of information this time of year so that when you get in the season, you know, who can handle what match-ups. For him, he's definitely done something probably every practice where you're like, "Wow, he did a great job there." Or he stood out. Um And that's really what you're looking for. Um now that being said, he's also made some big mistakes, too, you know, and it's like, man, um how much of that can you weather? Well, when you're talking about the punt team, not a lot, you know, so those guys got to go out there and execute. They got to protect the passer. It's going to be a blitz most of the time that they're picking up and they got to be 100%. Um and you can't have a sack or for us a blocked punt. So anyway, hey. >> [laughter] >> State. Uh so anyway, yeah, uh he's done some good things. Um and I would say he's right in the middle of a competition. The The advantage those other guys have is they've played so they've been through that stuff. I think Belichick, you know, I love Belichick, but he used to have a thing where there'd be no rookies playing on the punt team, you know, he just didn't didn't want that to happen because he knew a mistake in that phase is devastating. Um so if if anytime you have to put a young player out there like that, you got to be careful. Um and that's his challenge that he's fighting. The other guys have experience, but you know, they haven't in some ways flashed as much as he has at certain things, too, so um it'll be interesting. >> So Sorry, man. >> Oh, no, you're good. >> So the probably about half the league doesn't have both kick returner and punt returner playing the same the same guy playing both positions. Just curious why you why you think that is and do you believe maybe you have a guy here that can do both of those things? >> Yeah, well, I would say number one is on kick return you have to have two players back there. So, it can't just be the punt returner anyway. So, the punt returner may be a part of that, but he may not. I think it really just depends on the roster, the makeup, who you have. I do know that like if you were asking me preference, I would say I would like a bigger, stronger guy on kickoff return. And most of that's just durability. I mean, those guys take some shots. And I would say there's a little bit more contact with those guys. It's a little bit more like a run play than it is ball out in space. That's a little bit more like a punt return. So, it's definitely difficult to find a guy who does both. That being said, it also depends on the makeup of your roster. You might have a top wideout or one of your top wideouts you want to return punts, but you don't want them to return kickoffs. That could be part of that decision. So, a lot that goes into it. >> Who else could play that role? >> Yeah, I think, you know, Dorsett's done a little bit of both. He's done more punt return than kickoff return, but he's certainly done both there. I think TK can do some of both. We've seen him do that for us, too. So, you're talking about two guys who could do that. Then it also for us would turn back to who else do we have available on game day and what's the best combination 11 we can get. And in that conversation now, you know, I know he's not out there right now, but does Pacheco figure into that? You know, does somebody like that? Now, maybe you could have Pacheco and whoever that other running back is back there and you get two running back bodies and you don't play the punt returner back there. So, just always to make the best 11 and also play the best you can throughout the course of the whole season, too, not just any one game. >> What do you see as the biggest benefit to to having that operation with the with the holder, the snapper, and the kicker not going into three third season? I see it's pretty rare that that you return those guys. There's not maybe a little bit of turnover there. Just the the biggest benefit of that. >> Yeah, it's obviously great having all three of those guys back. I think you know how I feel about all three of them. I think all three are great players. They're very passionate about what they do, and they really work hard and become better every year and really every day, which I love. Um but yes, it's a benefit to them because now, you know, they can get in a good rhythm and routine, work together, they know each other's idiosyncrasies, the nuances. Um you're not adjusting your rhythm for a different snapper and things like that. So, I think it's helpful for them, too, but it's also comforting for us. >> Gibbs, can you expand a little bit on what you like about Pacheco beyond the body type as as a kick returner and then not just that return but on special teams. What does What does Jacob Saylors mean to you on special teams? >> Yeah, um so Pacheco, I mean, no, he did a little bit of it when he was younger in Kansas City, so he's seen that. He had some good plays back there. Um more than anything, you just watch him run the ball on offense. Like I think Gibbs would make a good returner, too. >> But uh um anyways, but yeah, so anytime if a guy's dynamic with the ball in his hands on offense and there's a chance that translates um on special teams, too. And uh so that's kind of really what we see in Pacheco. Obviously, when he gets healthy, maybe we can get him back there. And then some of it depends on his role on the roster and game day and etc. and playing the course 17 years or 17 games and all that. Um and then Saylors, I mean, I I love Saylors. I loved him a year ago. He came in and really helped us out um on special teams and I thought he played very, very well for us on teams a year ago. Um and then to see him go out there and play like that on offense, I was super happy for him in the last preseason game cuz to me he is a deserving kid of that attention. He really has gone under the radar but been a very good player for us on special teams um last year. So, I'm encouraged with that for him. >> And seeing this kind of massive It won't give you Gibbs as a return man, huh? >> Yeah, I don't know. When you put the ball in his hands, a lot happens, so I know that, so. >> So, we've seen kind of this massive developmental jump from Ahmad Gardner on defense. Seems like special teams, there's a lot more precision and control needed with with a player like that. How have you seen his his growth with with your groups in particular? >> Yeah, he does a great job. I mean, the one thing about him is that he goes out there and he works his tail off. He's going to fight and compete and you love that about him. He's tough as heck and he's very very competitive. He takes everything personal. >> [snorts] >> But you know, one thing that is a challenge for him on special teams, a lot of our plays are wide open space plays. You know, when you're playing defensive line, you're in a tighter confined box. We've utilized some players like that in the past on kickoff coverage here. So maybe that's an area he can help us out. But really when you're talking like punt punt return, it's going to be difficult. And then can you match up a guy on kickoff return? Defenders are used to getting away from blocks, not blocking as much. So some some guys are better at that than others. And he's definitely worked out of for us. So those types of players to me are more luxury type players. Like if he's available on game day and he made the roster and he's on the team and he's playing and the defense wants him. Could I find a role for him that would help elevate the players around him and make him one of the best 11 guys to be on the field on any given play? Then yeah, that's to me like a luxury. Those other linebackers, man, those guys got to play. You just don't have any other bodies. So certain positions kind of more viable to me than others. I would consider that one a luxury, but love what he does. >> So you kind of joking around with Jameson when he was walking around the field the other day. The the social team also put out a clip where you were wearing his jewelry and I'm just curious what kind of trickle down effect his joy has on the rest of the team from your perspective. >> Yeah, I mean he I mean Jamo's awesome. You guys know I've always loved him. I love the fact that he played gunner. You guys gave me hell because we were going to play him as a gunner. But, but no, I love him. He loves the game of football, you know, and I would say that's probably the biggest thing. You know, you're looking for guys who can stand out or make an impact or jump off the film and do it. You know, the only way I could relate it to you in this offseason or actually not too long ago. Chris Stapleton played a concert in Ford Field. So, I went to the concert and there's all these people leading up to it. The first guy, I don't know what his name something Allen or Allen Stone or something like that was incredible. Chris Stapleton obviously when you hear the guy sing live, you're like, "Oh my gosh, he just jumps off the stage." Lainey Wilson, I'm a huge Lainey Wilson fan. I think she's incredible. I love her story. I feel like she's just one of those people who made it on her own. And then I'm watching the Lainey Wilson show though and there was somebody comes up and this lady was jamming on this guitar and I'm like, "Damn, who is that?" And then all of a sudden she's playing the electric violin in front of everybody and this person jumped off the stage. The way she was playing that instrument with the passion and energy and I'm like, "Damn, I mean this is she's got it. I mean she has definitely got it." So, I looked up her name. Her name was Sevyn Streeter. She's from Traverse City, Michigan and I'm like, "Dude, she's got it." And really that's what you're looking for in a player. So, like Jamo, he's got it, man. Gibbs, he's got it. You put the ball in their hand, it jumps off the film, you see it. And that's what you're looking for in players, man. This time of year who can jump off the film and make you go, "Gosh darn it, like I got to look that person up. Who are they? I want them on this roster." That helps you. >> On teams for you, who's jumped off the film on teams for you? >> So, Tay Martin's jumped off the film every day. Bunch of these guys, Hunter's jumped off the film doing something good. Botchy's played some good football. All these guys I've mentioned, Reader's done some good things, you know. And that's why I say it's a very competitive situation here. Um but uh yeah, it's a good question. I can't give it all away.

text: Welcome back to another episode of Lions Collective. Jeff Idra, Justin Rogers, Will Burgefield, Colton Palency, the crew is back and we have a lot to get into. We'll talk about some players to watch uh in preseason game two. >> Love it. Hey, before we dive into that stuff, I want to take everyone sort of inside a conversation that I was having with Colton today on the sidelines watching practice. He said, you know, I just have to remind myself every single day not to take that guy for granted. And you know, I had the opportunity um will I don't I don't know if you were in the mix during Kelvin Johnson's career. Feel like you were >> No, my first year was post Calvin. >> Oh, okay. Okay. So I I had the opportunity to watch Calvin Johnson in practice every day and it's kind of the same thing and and different in some way because Calvin was a physical marvel and he would do those jaw-dropping things like practice after practice and you start to just get used to it and watching St. Brown this practice like the the greatness is just so absurd and for him it's just this extreme technical proficiency. Like I've said this before, I don't know if I've said it directly to any of you guys, but like I don't know how many players in the NFL squeeze more out of their physical ability than St. Brown. Like everything is just so precise, so crisp. Um, Hall of Fame element of the discussion super interesting because, you know, I know there are people that'll say too many people get led into Hall of Fame. I think it's really tough, really tough to get into the NFL Hall of Fame at five a year given the fact that we know that there are 50 guys in a roster. And um you know, I'll go back to And Sue, who was in five years in Detroit, a three-time first team allpro uh defensive rookie of the year, absolutely dominant, and looked every bit like he was going to roll into a Hall of Fame career. And um you know, Sue might make the Hall of Fame. I I don't know, but it's it's certainly not going to be a a first time through. It it might take him 10, 15 years. I don't know. Uh and so I I I think at some point I'm still recognizing that we're only seeing small stretches of these guys' career so far. Uh the Hall of Fame largely is about sustaining it over a long period of time. But I will say if this group is the group that gets the Lions over the hump as a Super Bowl winner, like that cherry on top will will be very favorable when their when their candidacy comes up. But right now, I mean, >> if we're talking about future Hall of Famers, like S, St. Brown, Hudson, Gibbs are are all kind of like on a very very early trajectory. But again, I think St. Brown's going to have to do it for five, six, seven more years just given the the receiving numbers that we see here. Justin, I think you make a great point, too, like we should also remember exactly how challenging it is to make the Hall of Fame. It's not just about being great, it's about being great for a decade plus. And, you know, I I think Colton's point is like there's a difference obviously between Hall of Fame career and Hall of Fame talent. We we use the word Hall of Fame. I think Hall of Fame trajectory is probably more accurate here. Just, you know, looking at the scope of talent they have all at once and the fact that all these guys are under contract for a long time and they're part of the core here. So nothing ever just like oh my god, I can't believe that happened. But how often does something happen that you boy, I I didn't think that team would do that and this is where in a spot you know, that you want to have that cap room you're talking about because somebody comes available, be it by trade, cut, or what have you, that you can swoop in and get. How often do you kind of get surprised by what someone else does? >> Sure. Well, I, you know, having done this for a long time, I think more than you'd think. Uh so, retaining flexibility to be able to entertain the unforeseen is an important aspect of how we try to structure our cap management philosophy. To pre We really want to present coach and Brett with uh the flexibility to entertain smart roster moves that are independent of uh cap constraints that we may have. We certainly have some of them, uh but we don't have a perfect crystal ball, none of us in the front office, and think opportunities present themselves that are unforeseen. So, uh yeah, we plan to be flexible. Uh there are limits to that given that we have a lot of good players under contract, but we try to present Brett and coach with opportunities uh through our cap management. >> Last couple. >> Going more into that and how it pertains to Patrick, I mean, honestly, you know, you've got one of the highest-paid quarterbacks in the game after you restructured him this last summer, he becomes the highest-paid guy, but also still trying to build out the rest of your roster. >> Sure. Uh well, first of all, uh I think as Clark and coach and Brett alluded to when we did the contract extension in June, uh he's an elite player and an even better person. Uh we were delighted to be able to once again extend him here, and we have a special relationship with him. Obviously, he is the highest-paid player in the league. Uh he's earned that, uh and we have a plan to manage around it. Uh the fact that that uh we have certainty around the quarterback allows us to plan how to allocate the rest of our resources in a way that gives us a lot of stability and ability to predict how we can move in the future. >> Last one, anyone? >> Thanks, Chris. >> Thank you very much.

Yeah, I mean I I obviously, you know, there there's there's nobody's expectations that exceed higher than mine. And, you know, I've always been my hardest critic. No, I I always say it to, you know, everyone that asks me like I don't think I could have really got a better vet than than him being in the room. How have you told the line between you know showing it but not going too far? title: Breaking down Colts’ signing of WR Keenan Allen
text: While you may have been asleep, the Colts made arguably the team's biggest free agency signing of the entire off-season, coming to terms with uh veteran wide receiver Keenan Allen on a one-year deal, according to our fellow Colts insider Joel A. Erickson, uh an incentive-laden deal worth up to 8.32 million dollars. Let's break it all down. Um this has been a move that the Colts fans and even media, uh myself included, have been in clamoring for for months. Um if you think back to where the Colts offense was 12 months ago, um they not only had Michael Pittman Jr., um who you would say was the the team's number two wide receiver throughout the 2025 season. They also had um up-and-coming wideout AD Mitchell, um the fourth guy on the depth chart. They traded away both of those wideouts in the span of um just a couple months. Um AD Mitchell in the middle of the 2025 season, Michael Pittman Jr. in March ahead of the start of free agency. And through the entire off-season, we've been waiting for the Colts to add another starting-caliber wide receiver to this unit, um alongside Alec Pierce, who is of course yet to um hit the practice field this off-season as he continues to rehab a late March ankle surgery. And uh slot receiver Josh Downs, along with star starting tight end Tyler Warren. Throughout training camp, we have seen the Colts um work through uh veteran wide receiver Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, the only wide receiver that the Colts signed outside the organization this off-season in free agency. Um we've seen Laquon Treadwell, a former first-round pick and a 10-year veteran in the league, get some first-team reps. And we've also seen Ashton Dulin, um the Colts long-time special teams ace, who's only caught seven passes over the the 2 years, also get those first-team reps. Laquon Treadwell has not caught a pass in the NFL in 2 years. Nick Westbrook-Ikhine only caught 11 passes last year in a 1-year stint with the Miami Dolphins. So, a combination of three guys who are fighting for that third wide receiver spot that to those on the outside have really not felt like the caliber of receiver that the the Colts need to get that offense back up to the level that it once was at the first half of last season. Now, with Keenan Allen, they have that fixed. Um a much cheaper option, a guy who had almost identical numbers to Michael Pittman Jr. last year. A player who routinely has 60, 70, 80 catches over the course of his career. At least 740 yards over the last 9 years of his career, somewhere between four and seven touchdowns or so. Just a very reliable short-distance receiver. A guy who can be a little bit of a possession receiver, get you first downs, fight for yardage over the middle of the field. Be the the type of receiver frankly that Michael Pittman Jr. was in lots of ways. A receiver that the Colts didn't really have on the roster without him. Now that he is on the roster, those guys fighting for that third spot now fight for that fourth spot. The Colts get a lot better at depth. It now becomes much more difficult for defenses to take away the passing game when you have four threats that you can put on the field at one time. Anyone can go off on any given day. We saw a lot of that last year where Alec Pierce or Josh Downs or Michael Pittman Jr. or Tyler Warren could lead the Colts on any given day. That does take away some volume from some of those guys. You have to be selfless enough to play in an offense where you have great guys around you, but with Daniel Jones, a healthy Daniel Jones I might add, who's looked all in all pretty solid in training camp along with this addition of Keenan Allen still just short of a month ahead of the start of the regular season. Um, while we still wait for Alec Pierce to return to the practice field, a very good move to bolster the strength and the depth of this offense. It felt like that was the the last remaining piece that we could realistically expect for the Colts to add before the start of the season. We see them make it and we will see what comes from that. The Colts will be back on the field on Wednesday and Thursday for a pair of joint practices with Falcons ahead of Saturday's preseason game against Atlanta at Lucas Oil Stadium. We Joel and I will have a podcast where we talk about this Keenan Allen news. We will have some stories from training camp. I I encourage you to go check out our news story and my insider story on the Keenan Allen signing on indystar.com and we'll have a lot more for you on that and the rest of Colts training camp on indystar.com in the next couple days. Thanks for watching.

Do you internally with the standard that you guys have here like you got everything out of practice today? >> Oh, yeah, most definitely. I mean, it was some good, it was some bad, and we got to clean it up. But like I said, I think for our first joint practice, man, I thought we looked really good, man. Like I said, it's going to be a lot of stuff on tape that we have to look and get better at. But for our first time coming out as a group, coming out as a defense, man, I was really proud of the guys, man. We just got to keep, you know, climbing that climbing that tree, keep chopping wood, and keep getting better. >> You guys put a lot of pressure on the quarterbacks, you and Clelin. When you are out there, and you're rushing, you know that on the other side, Crosby's doing the same thing. Is it kind of like a little bit of a motivation that this other rusher like you guys going one on one out there? >> It's crazy cuz me and Clelin kind of talked about that this offseason, but I like obviously I have a ton of respect for Max, and Max is big bro. Me and him talk a a bunch all the time, and he's been really great for me. Um, but honestly like I know he's over there, but me I was like, "Bro, I'm also worried about the tackles." You know what I'm saying? Or what I'm going against. And we always catch up after practice and see how that went, but a ton of respect for Max, man. He's a awesome player in this league, one of the top guys in this league. So I look up to him, man, but um, you know, when me and Clelin are at the front, we always say when we get in that three-point stance, and I look down at the ball, and I see Clelin over there, it just gives me so much confidence cuz I know I'm out there with my dog. >> I know that you got a bunch of practices today as well with Logan and with Clelin. Do you see how this defense can be creative? >> Yeah, man, both of those guys, I'll start with Logan first. I think he's going to unlock so much. Both of those guys are going to unlock so much for what we want to do with this front, and uh, things that we can do defensively to get a lot of guys going. Um, both of those guys rush really well, and I I can't wait to see how we use them. >> Clelin said something interesting last week um, when talking about you. He said like, uh, you know, the difference between you when you were a rookie and now is like you now have the ability to flip a switch where you can just take over a game. >> Yeah. >> Do you agree with that? Like how And and how has that evolved over time? >> Yeah, man, my confidence has been like really high, uh but it it's not because of the check or anything like that. It's just more so because I've seen the preparation and the consistency that I've been going through all off season and now in camp. And I've seen my pass rush grow, I've seen my run game grow, I've seen I've grown as a leader, and it just gives me so much confidence and when I step on the practice field and I step into these games or step into joint practice, I have that much confidence because I prepared the right way, I've trained my body right way, I put my body in those positions to be able to go make the plays that I need to play or be in positions that my coach needs me to be in. >> We've got a couple more after this. >> How pleased have you been with McDonald from start of OTAs to now, especially now going up against Golden Tate? >> Man, I've been really pleased with him, man. He's grown a lot over these last couple of months, man. Got his body in good shape. His mindset's getting there, man, and he's been leaning on us big time. And he's been learning the system. Um he's been good taking care of his body. So, like I said, we told him we we we we need you. You're going to be playing a lot for us, man, and he's taking that as a challenge and he's gotten better every single practice. You you always talk about the physical side. But talk about the the mental matrix that go up your practice rep by rep, especially with the way you're going against this team. >> Yeah, most definitely. Mentally, it's taking yourself to that zone. Mentally, it's taking yourself to that place where like you won't be denied. We have a saying like leave no doubt. And I think that's our mentality, man. Let's go ahead and put it on their mind right now. Let's leave no doubt about who we are as a defense, who we are as a D-lineman. Come out here with the right mentality, come out here and work.
